questions.prompt: What does the MVVM acronym stand for in software architecture?

options.text: Model-View-ViewModel
options.explanation: MVVM stands for Model, View, and ViewModel.

options.text: Main-View-Variable-Manager
options.explanation: This is a fabricated phrase and not a real design pattern.

options.text: Model-Value-View-Module
options.explanation: This phrase does not match the MVVM architectural pattern.

options.text: Mobile-View-Version-Manager
options.explanation: This phrase is incorrect.

questions.prompt: Which primary responsibility belongs to the Model layer in MVVM?

options.text: Drawing shapes and borders on the screen
options.explanation: Visual drawing is handled by the View layer.

options.text: Holding raw domain data and business rules
options.explanation: The Model represents domain entities, data schemas, and core business rules.

options.text: Listening directly to screen tap gestures
options.explanation: Touch events and gestures are captured by the View.

options.text: Formatting currency and dates for labels
options.explanation: Presentation formatting belongs to the ViewModel.

questions.prompt: What is the main role of the View layer in MVVM?

options.text: Storing raw user credentials in disk databases
options.explanation: Storage and persistence belong in domain models or services.

options.text: Executing remote HTTP networking calls
options.explanation: Network calls belong in network service objects, not views.

options.text: Rendering the user interface and forwarding user events
options.explanation: The View displays controls and forwards user actions to the ViewModel.

options.text: Computing complex statistical data algorithms
options.explanation: Complex calculations belong in domain models or service layers.

questions.prompt: Why does a ViewModel avoid importing UIKit or SwiftUI view rendering types?

options.text: Because Swift does not permit importing UI frameworks inside classes
options.explanation: Swift permits importing UI frameworks in any file, but architecture forbids it here.

options.text: Because UI frameworks can only be imported in structs
options.explanation: Classes in UIKit regularly import UIKit.

options.text: Because ViewModels compile directly into database instructions
options.explanation: ViewModels are normal Swift classes.

options.text: To keep presentation logic decoupled and fast to unit test
options.explanation: Excluding UI frameworks allows quick unit tests without simulator dependencies.

questions.prompt: When a user taps a button in an MVVM screen, what is the first step in the data flow?

options.text: The View forwards the user intent to the ViewModel
options.explanation: The View delegates user actions directly to methods on its ViewModel.

options.text: The View modifies the database on disk immediately
options.explanation: The View should never directly modify persistent storage.

options.text: The Model calls a redraw method on the View
options.explanation: The Model does not know about the View.

options.text: The operating system restarts the view lifecycle
options.explanation: Tapping a button triggers an event handler, not a lifecycle restart.

questions.prompt: Which macro introduced in iOS 17 is commonly used to make a ViewModel observable?

options.text: @Model
options.explanation: @Model is a SwiftData macro for persistent data storage.

options.text: @Observable
options.explanation: @Observable makes classes observable by SwiftUI views without manual wrappers.

options.text: @Published
options.explanation: @Published is a Combine property wrapper, not an iOS 17 macro.

options.text: @StateObject
options.explanation: @StateObject is a property wrapper used with Combine ObservableObject.

questions.prompt: Why should a ViewModel driving UI updates be annotated with @MainActor?

options.text: To force the class to be stored in read-only memory
options.explanation: MainActor isolation manages thread execution, not memory read permissions.

options.text: To prevent other objects from calling its methods
options.explanation: MainActor restricts concurrency, not general accessibility.

options.text: To guarantee all published UI state mutations occur on the main thread
options.explanation: UI updates must execute on the main thread to avoid data races and UI glitches.

options.text: To automatically convert all integer numbers into strings
options.explanation: MainActor does not perform data conversions.

questions.prompt: Where should date formatting and string localization occur in an MVVM architecture?

options.text: Inside the backend database query
options.explanation: Databases store raw data, not localized presentation strings.

options.text: Inside the raw domain Model struct
options.explanation: Domain models remain agnostic of user presentation and locale formatting.

options.text: Inside the SwiftUI view body on every render pass
options.explanation: Formatting in the body causes repeated calculations during rendering.

options.text: Inside the ViewModel, providing ready-to-display properties
options.explanation: The ViewModel owns presentation logic, formatting raw data into display strings.

questions.prompt: How does a SwiftUI View typically hold its primary ViewModel in modern SwiftUI?

options.text: Using @State var viewModel = ProductViewModel()
options.explanation: Using @State with an @Observable class ensures SwiftUI maintains the object across view updates.

options.text: Using a global singleton variable
options.explanation: Global singletons harm testability and view reusability.

options.text: Using a weak var reference without ownership
options.explanation: A weak reference would deallocate the ViewModel immediately.

options.text: Using @Binding var viewModel: ProductViewModel
options.explanation: Bindings are for sharing value mutations, not owning top-level view models.

questions.prompt: What is the Massive ViewModel anti-pattern?

options.text: Using a ViewModel that takes up too much disk storage space
options.explanation: The problem relates to code responsibilities, not compiled binary size.

options.text: Dumping networking, routing, and database code into the ViewModel
options.explanation: Placing all app responsibilities into one ViewModel repeats the Massive View Controller mistake.

options.text: Allocating multiple view models on the heap at once
options.explanation: Allocating multiple small view models is normal and expected.

options.text: Creating view models using class inheritance instead of structs
options.explanation: ViewModels are commonly classes to maintain identity and observation.

questions.prompt: How should an engineer avoid creating a Massive ViewModel?

options.text: Combine all screens of the app into a single view controller
options.explanation: This makes the code much worse.

options.text: Move all networking code directly into SwiftUI view bodies
options.explanation: Views should focus exclusively on UI presentation.

options.text: Inject separate service and repository objects into the ViewModel
options.explanation: Delegating networking, caching, and persistence to services keeps ViewModels lean.

options.text: Delete all unit tests to simplify the codebase
options.explanation: Deleting unit tests harms code quality.

questions.prompt: When is creating a ViewModel considered unnecessary over-engineering?

options.text: When a screen requires complex asynchronous networking
options.explanation: Async networking and state handling benefit greatly from a ViewModel.

options.text: When multiple buttons trigger distinct business actions
options.explanation: Multiple business actions warrant a dedicated ViewModel.

options.text: When presentation formatting must be verified in unit tests
options.explanation: Unit testing presentation logic is a core reason to use a ViewModel.

options.text: When a simple SwiftUI view only displays static text or local state
options.explanation: Static views or trivial forms work cleanly with native SwiftUI state without extra layers.

questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview
questions.prompt: How does MVVM compare to Apple MVC in terms of unit testability?

options.text: MVVM tests presentation logic easily without UI dependencies
options.explanation: MVC tightly couples presentation to UIViewController lifecycles, while MVVM isolates presentation logic.

options.text: MVC is easier to test because view controllers run in memory without views
options.explanation: View controllers are coupled to UIKit lifecycles and view loading.

options.text: MVVM requires UI test automation for all verification
options.explanation: MVVM enables fast headless unit testing.

options.text: Both patterns have identical test coverage boundaries
options.explanation: MVVM decouples logic from view lifecycles, providing superior testability.

questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview
questions.prompt: How should navigation between screens be handled when building an app with MVVM?

options.text: ViewModels should present view controllers directly using UIKit methods
options.explanation: ViewModels should not import UIKit or manage view hierarchies.

options.text: Navigation should be delegated to routers, coordinators, or navigation paths
options.explanation: Coordinators or navigation paths isolate screen transitions away from view models.

options.text: Models should handle modal presentation logic
options.explanation: Models must have no awareness of screens or navigation.

options.text: Navigation is not possible when using MVVM
options.explanation: MVVM is widely used with coordinators and navigation stacks.

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental benefit of unidirectional data flow in MVVM?

options.text: It eliminates the need for unit tests
options.explanation: Unidirectional data flow improves testability but does not replace tests.

options.text: It speeds up network download speeds automatically
options.explanation: Data flow architecture has no impact on network hardware speed.

options.text: State changes are predictable because user events flow in one direction
options.explanation: Predictable flow from View to ViewModel to Model and back simplifies debugging and testing.

options.text: It allows models to render views directly without intermediate layers
options.explanation: Models never render views in MVVM.
